newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain shapes up for Euro with austere budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain shapes up for Euro with austere budget.

text.p: Spain's government approved a stringent 1997 budget on Friday that shapes up the nation for the launch of Europe's single currency in 1999 and should pave the way for another reduction in official interest rates.

"(We promised) an austere budget that would accomplish the goals important to Spaniards. This is that budget," said Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato, presenting the broad outlines of the draft to journalists following cabinet approval.

The five-month-old minority Popular Party government faced the thorny problem of reducing the deficit to the common currency regime's reference value of three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from 6.6 percent in 1995.
It also had to cut Spanish debt to GDP to 60 percent from 66 percent in 1995 or at least take steps to reduce it. Rato said the government complied.
"The public deficit will be at three percent and public debt will be declining," Rato said, adding that the government had achieved its goals without resorting to any creative accounting.

To slash the 1.2 billion pesetas ($9.37 million) in spending necessary, the budget foresees a cap on spending growth at 1.7 percent in 1997, better than the two percent it had forecast earlier, and far beneath expected inflation of 2.6 percent.
Revenues are seen growing by just under six percent. In total 1997 budget expenditures are seen at 18.1 trillion pesetas, with income at 16.1 trillion.

Financial markets, which have skyrocketed this month in expectation of a solid budget, gave the draft their stamp of approval, convinced the Bank of Spain could now sanction its sixth interest rate cut of the year at its next regular repo.
"Rato said what we hoped he would say, he didn't surprise us," said Alfredo Urrutia, capital markets economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

"The market liked the fact that he said the numbers he was supposed to say...A cut of 25 basis points is already discounted, now we can see even 50 basis points because of the strength of the peseta."
The Bank of Spain has reduced its key money market rate to the current 7.25 percent from nine percent at the beginning of January and financial market experts see the next reduction on October 3.
Markets pulled back slightly on the news, with bonds coming off highs and the bourse extending losses.

But the slight retreat did not dent the month's gains. Spanish bond futures prices have soared more than six full points since the end of August, while yields on the 10-year benchmark bond have dropped sixty basis points.
The peseta continues its battle to break through 84.00 marks, and dealers say the only thing checking it is the Bank of Spain buying marks for pesetas.
The government will officially present the draft to parliament on Monday. It has already secured the support from its loose coalition partners to win the budget's approval.
